A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support matching retained experiments against the substantially revised theoretical material.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic recovery and scalability experiments, semi-synthetic concept-recovery results, and LLM activation evaluations, including SAEBench results and appendix ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results in Section 5 and Appendices A.3–A.5, including numerical comparisons, statistical analyses, and qualitative concept-relation examples.

M1.justification: The linear encoder/decoder, residual noise estimation, Laplace-based loss, and sparsity penalties on temporal and instantaneous relations are retained. v2 foregrounds the lower-triangular restriction on M, but this constraint was already documented in v1 Appendix A.2.1; the PDFs do not establish an algorithm change.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same synthetic processes, Pile legal/XML/email collections, five word-pair categories, and Pythia/Gemma activation tasks. The longer-lag and pretrained-SAE investigations already appear in v1's appendix.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains SAE+regression, and Table 2 retains ReLU SAE and TopK SAE. The scalability discussion retains IDOL and iCITRIS. No evaluated comparator is added or removed.

E3.justification: The synthetic generators, evaluation metrics, training budgets, latent dimensions, temporal lags, and preprocessing remain unchanged. The 300M/500M-token extended training and lag-100 investigation are present in both appendices; new theoretical assumptions do not establish changed experimental settings.

E4.justification: v1 Appendix A.4 and v2 Appendix A.5 contain the same training-dynamics analyses, TopK and sparsity comparisons, alpha/beta sensitivity studies, bias ablation, extended-lag investigation, and pretrained-SAE case studies. The new examination of a proof belongs to theory rather than empirical supplementary analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions disclose seeds 123, 456, and 789 and retain the same statistical procedures: 100 samples per method for equivalence testing, Welch–TOST and Hodges–Lehmann tests, and absorption confidence intervals based on at least 200 samples. No run-count or uncertainty-reporting practice changes.

E6.justification: The numerical and qualitative empirical findings are retained. For example, Table 1 reports the same proposed-method scores of 19.95, 8.63, and 2.66 against SAE+regression's 0.54, 0.94, and 0.74. SAEBench scores, appendix ablation tables, recovery plots, steering correlations, and relation examples also match.

T1.justification: v1 derives its linear identifiability proposition from cited nonlinear theorems and supplies a componentwise-linear proof in Appendix A.1. v2 argues that the required variability assumption fails, replaces that foundation with an autocovariance/non-Gaussianity theorem, and adds componentwise and subspace-identifiability corollaries with new rank, stability, and structural assumptions. Appendices A.1–A.2 replace the previous proof with a failure analysis and a new derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same central contributions: jointly modeling temporal and instantaneous concept relations, providing identifiability guarantees, achieving scalability, and demonstrating synthetic and LLM applications. The conclusion retains these scientific claims despite the replacement of their theoretical support.

C2.justification: v2 withdraws the interpretation that the earlier nonlinear guarantees directly establish linear recovery. It explains general invertible ambiguity and distinguishes stronger conditions for componentwise recovery from subspace recovery. It also removes v1's justification for extending invertibility to overcomplete sparse representations. These materially revise the explanation of the guarantees' applicability, although the dedicated limitations section is retained.

D1.justification: v1 Appendix A.5 directs readers to a supplementary-material folder; v2 Appendix A.6 supplies a specific GitHub repository for reproducing the experiments. This changes the documented access instructions. Hardware, optimization, preprocessing, and training details otherwise remain the same; repository availability was not independently checked.

R1.justification: The central theoretical lineage is repositioned: v1 presents its result as a linear consequence of Li et al.'s nonlinear identifiability results, whereas v2 explains their inapplicability and positions its theorem as extending Zhang and Hyvarinen's 2011 linear non-Gaussian model. The two dictionary-learning references supporting the former overcomplete argument are removed. The broader related-work survey is largely retained.

P1.justification: The theoretical exposition is substantially reorganized from definitions, borrowed theorems, and a linear proposition into a theorem–proof–discussion sequence with two corollaries. The appendix separates diagnosis of the previous argument from the replacement proof. Smaller edits condense passages, update cross-references, trim the conclusion, and add acknowledgments; most experimental prose remains intact.

P2.justification: The existing figures and tables are retained, with localized resizing, repositioning, and text reflow. Figure 2 moves within the implementation discussion, Figures 7 and 8 are reduced in size, and Table 1 changes position relative to surrounding text. No new empirical display or substantive redesign is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 usefully identifies why v1's inherited sufficient-variability argument fails, states more explicit assumptions, and provides clearer code-access instructions. However, the central theoretical repair remains unresolved as written: Theorem 1 assumes equivalence of autocovariances, while Appendix A.2 Step 4 uses stronger equivalence of generated processes to obtain the signed-permutation conclusion. With empirical evidence unchanged, the transparency gains do not establish that the main identifiability deficiency has been repaired, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.
